summary: Fouad Matin explains that frontier research labs are pushing coding benchmarks and deployability, making every agent effectively a code-executing agent. Code helps across the stack, not just for software engineering tasks, including multimodal reasoning like OCR. This represents a paradigm shift: instead of complex inner loops where models determine task type and load specific prompts and tools, models now decide when to use tools and write/run code autonomously. From a security perspective, this is Remote Code Execution (RCE). Key risks include prompt injection and data exfiltration (top priority), accidental mistakes like installing malicious packages or writing vulnerable code, privilege escalation, and sandbox escapes. OpenAI's preparedness framework requires safeguards to avoid misalignment at large-scale deployment. Three primary safeguards are discussed. (1) Sandboxing—ideally giving the agent its own isolated computer (as with Codex and ChatGPT containers producing PRs); for local execution, using containerization, app-level, or OS-level sandboxing. Codex CLI is fully open-sourced, demonstrating Mac OS 'seatbelt' sandboxing (inspired by Chromium) and Linux seccomp/landlock sandboxing in Rust. (2) Disabling/limiting internet access—the highest-probability vector for prompt injection. Codex CLI offers 'full auto' mode restricting file access and network calls; Codex/ChatGPT now support configurable allow lists with HTTP method restrictions. (3) Human review—using watch mode monitoring and reviewing final diffs; LLM-based code review helps but is not a substitute for human oversight. For building agents, Fouad recommends deferring logic to the reasoning model with appropriate tools: local shell (released in the API for training models to write and execute code), apply_patch (for applying diffs without precise line numbers), MCP, and web search. An example combines Socket's dependency vulnerability checking MCP server to verify dependencies before installation. OpenAI is releasing a container service as part of its agents SDK and responses API, runnable locally or hosted by OpenAI. The recap emphasizes sandboxing, thoughtful internet management, and requiring human review. LM-based monitors are valuable but not yet sufficient for deterministic certainty. More tooling and documentation are planned in the Codex repo. OpenAI is hiring for the Agent Robustness and Control team and for Rust engineers to build Codex CLI integrations.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Every frontier agent is becoming a code-executing agent, not just for SWE tasks but across the entire stack including multimodal reasoning
Autonomous code execution is effectively Remote Code Execution (RCE) from a security perspective, requiring careful guardrails at every layer
Prompt injection and data exfiltration are the top-priority security risks; untrusted content from docs or GitHub issues can leak into the agent's trusted inner loop
Sandboxing is the first safeguard—ideally give the agent its own isolated computer; for local execution use containerization, app-level, or OS-level sandboxing
Internet access is the highest-probability vector for prompt injection; Codex CLI offers 'full auto' sandboxed mode and Codex/ChatGPT support configurable allow lists with HTTP method restrictions
Combining model-level controls (flagging suspicious behavior) with system-level controls (deterministic network restrictions) is key to solving prompt injection
Human review of final diffs and operations is essential; LLM-based monitors are valuable but not yet a substitute for deterministic controls
OpenAI provides tools for building agents: local shell (API), apply_patch (for diffs), MCP, and web search; agents should defer logic to the reasoning model with the right tools
OpenAI is releasing a container service in its agents SDK and responses API, runnable locally or OpenAI-hosted, strongly recommending remote containers for production
OpenAI is hiring for the Agent Robustness and Control team and for Rust engineers to expand Codex CLI integrations

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Fouad introduces himself, his background on OpenAI's security team and agent robustness, and his work on Codex and Codex CLI.

sections.title: Code-Executing Agents as the New Paradigm
sections.summary: Frontier labs are pushing coding benchmarks and deployability, making every agent a code-executing agent. Code helps across the stack, not just SWE tasks—e.g., multimodal reasoning with OCR and image cropping. The complex inner loop paradigm is shifting to autonomous tool and code use.

sections.title: Security Risks of Code Execution
sections.summary: Autonomous code execution is effectively RCE. Key risks: prompt injection and data exfiltration (top priority), accidental mistakes (malicious packages, vulnerable code), privilege escalation, sandbox escapes. OpenAI's preparedness framework requires safeguards to avoid misalignment at scale.

sections.title: Safeguard 1: Sandboxing
sections.summary: Best method: give the agent its own isolated computer (as with Codex/ChatGPT containers producing PRs). For local execution: containerization, app-level, or OS-level sandboxing. Codex CLI is open-sourced as a reference. Mac OS uses seatbelt (inspired by Chromium); Linux uses seccomp and landlock in Rust.

sections.title: Safeguard 2: Disabling/Limiting Internet Access
sections.summary: Internet access is the highest-probability vector for prompt injection. Codex CLI 'full auto' mode restricts file access and network calls. Codex/ChatGPT now support configurable allow lists with HTTP method restrictions. Example: prompt injection via GitHub issue comments can exfiltrate code. Combining model-level and system-level controls is key.

sections.title: Safeguard 3: Human Review
sections.summary: Human review of final diffs and operations is essential. Watch mode ensures a human reviews actions the agent takes. LLM-based code review tools help but don't substitute for human oversight. Operator browser agent uses domain lists and in-loop monitors for sensitive operations. Balancing maximum security with maximum flexibility is key.

sections.title: Building Agents and Future Work
sections.summary: For building agents, defer logic to the reasoning model and give it the right tools. OpenAI released local shell (in the API for training models to write/execute code), apply_patch (for applying diffs without precise line numbers), plus standard tools like MCP and web search. Example: Socket's dependency vulnerability checking MCP server lets agents verify dependencies before installation, with optional system-level post-rollout checks. OpenAI strongly recommends remote containers and is releasing a container service in its agents SDK and responses API (local or OpenAI-hosted). Recap: sandbox agents, thoughtfully manage internet access, require human review. LM-based monitors are valuable but not yet sufficient for deterministic certainty. More tooling and documentation planned in the Codex repo. OpenAI is hiring for the Agent Robustness and Control team and for Rust engineers to build Codex CLI integrations.

demonstrations: Codex CLI open-source sandboxing implementation using Mac OS seatbelt policy (inspired by Chromium)
Linux sandboxing in Rust using seccomp and landlock for unprivileged sandbox and preventing privilege escalation
Codex/ChatGPT container isolation: spins up a fully isolated container and produces a PR at the end
Codex CLI 'full auto' mode: agent can only read/write within its run directory, network calls only for auto-approved commands
Codex/ChatGPT configurable internet allow lists with HTTP method restrictions and risk warnings
Operator browser agent with domain lists and in-loop monitor for sensitive operations
Local shell tool released in the API for training models to write and execute code
apply_patch tool released for applying diffs to files without requiring precise line numbers
Socket MCP server example: expose dependency vulnerability checking to agent before installing packages, with system-level post-rollout verification option
Container service being released as part of agents SDK and responses API, runnable locally or OpenAI-hosted
limitations: Seatbelt documentation for Mac OS sandboxing is hard to find; required deep research and models to understand bounds of examples
Model-level controls for flagging suspicious behavior are still an area of focus in model training
Balancing review granularity between 'yolo mode' and approving every single command is not yet practical at either extreme
LM-based monitors in the loop are valuable but not yet sufficient for the certainty provided by deterministic controls
Models are not particularly good at getting line numbers correct for git diffs, necessitating apply_patch
